client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away six months ago. Family get-togethers used to feel warm and comforting, but now when I show up to them, I just feel... hollow, like I'm watching everyone else from behind glass. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the problem isn't really in my head — she's just gone, and nothing can fix that.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy — that sense of being present in body but somehow disconnected from everyone around you, like grief has put up an invisible wall. You're right that nothing will bring her back, and I want to honor that truth rather than talk around it. I'm curious, though — when you imagine what *would* feel like relief, even just a little, what comes to mind?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I don't know... maybe just not waking up in the morning and immediately feeling that weight before I've even opened my eyes. Like, there's this split second when I first wake up where I forget, and then it crashes back in, and that moment of forgetting almost makes it worse. I guess relief would be... being able to think about her without it feeling like I'm being hollowed out from the inside.
therapist: That image of the split second before it crashes back — that's such a painful and precise way to describe grief, and it tells me you've been sitting with this very closely and quietly. The way you're describing it, there's something that sounds almost exhausted underneath the words, like you've been holding this weight very carefully for a long time without letting it fully show. I wonder — is there anyone in your life right now with whom you don't have to hold it so carefully?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, no. There's no one I can really let it fall apart in front of — my friends knew her too, so when I'm around them I end up trying to manage their grief on top of my own, and that's somehow even more exhausting. And my family... they mean well, but they keep saying things like "she's in a better place" and I just have to nod and smile because I don't want to make it worse for them.
therapist: You've essentially become the caretaker of everyone else's grief while yours has nowhere to go — that's an enormous and lonely thing to carry. I notice as you're describing all of this there's a kind of rushing quality, like you're moving quickly through something that might be very painful to slow down inside of. What do you think would happen if, just for a moment, you let yourself *not* be okay with what they say — not out loud to them, but just honestly, here?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think if I actually let myself not be okay with it... I don't know, it feels like something would crack open and I wouldn't be able to put it back together. Like I've been holding this shape for so long that if I let it go, even just in here, I'm not sure who I am without it. And honestly, part of me is scared that if I start feeling how lonely this actually is, it'll just confirm that no one really sees me anyway.
therapist: What you just said about not knowing who you are without the grief — that's such an important and brave thing to notice, because it suggests this isn't just about losing her, it's also touching something deeper about feeling seen and known. And that fear that letting yourself feel the loneliness will only confirm no one really sees you — I want to gently push back on that, because the fact that you can name it so clearly, right here, right now, suggests a part of you is already being witnessed. What's it like to have said that out loud, even just to me?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess it feels... strange, saying it out loud. Like part of me is waiting for you to not really get it, to say something that makes me feel like I explained it wrong or you heard something different than what I meant. I don't know if being witnessed by a therapist counts the same way as being seen by someone who actually knows me and chooses to stay.
therapist: That distinction you're drawing is real and it matters — there's something different about being chosen by someone who knows your whole story, and I'm not going to pretend this is the same thing. But I'm also noticing that even as you say this, there's something that sounds a little braced, like you're already half-expecting to be disappointed here too — and I wonder if that pattern, of waiting for the moment you'll be misunderstood, shows up in those friendships and family moments as well. What would it look like to let someone in your life *try* to see you, even imperfectly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, you're probably right that I do that — kind of pre-emptively pull back before anyone gets close enough to let me down. But honestly, when I think about actually letting someone try, even imperfectly, I just picture all the ways it goes sideways — they say the wrong thing, or they get tired of me, or I can tell they don't really get it even if they're trying. It's like the bracing you're describing is the only thing that feels safe, even though I know it's also what keeps me so isolated.
therapist: You've just described the trap so clearly — the very thing that protects you is also what keeps you in that hollow, behind-the-glass feeling, and some part of you already knows that. I'm struck by how you're naming all of this with such clarity and yet your voice sounds almost quiet and small, like you're saying something true but from very far away. I'm curious — when you picture those ways it goes sideways, whose voice is it that tells you you'll be too much, or that they'll eventually leave?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That question kind of stops me, honestly. It's my mom's voice, I think — she had this way of going quiet and distant when I was too emotional or too needy, like I'd crossed some invisible line, and I learned pretty fast that being a lot was a problem. And I guess I've just... carried that voice around with me ever since, applying it to everyone before they even get the chance to prove me wrong.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — that voice wasn't the truth about you, it was a lesson you had to learn to stay close to her, and at the time it probably kept you safe. And I notice as you're saying this you're moving through it quite quickly, like you're reporting something important from a little bit of a distance — I wonder if there's something even more tender underneath that you haven't quite let yourself land on yet. What was it like to be that child, learning to make yourself smaller?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess... when you put it that way, it kind of catches me off guard. I've been telling myself this story about my mom for so long that it almost feels clinical now, like it happened to someone else. But if I actually try to sit with what it was like to be that kid... it's just really lonely, you know? Like no matter how small I made myself, it was never quite small enough.
therapist: That image of never being quite small enough — that's heartbreaking, and I want you to know that says everything about the impossible situation you were in, and nothing about your worth. I notice your voice has gone very soft as you're saying this, like you're holding something fragile, and I just want to stay here with you in it for a moment rather than move past it. That child deserved so much more space than they were given.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I didn't expect that to hit me so hard, but my eyes are stinging right now and I'm trying not to cry. It's strange because I've told that story before, or parts of it, and nobody's ever just... stopped like that. I don't really know what to do with someone actually sitting in it with me instead of rushing to fix it.
therapist: You don't have to do anything with it — you're allowed to just let it be there, tears and all. What you're describing, that no one has stopped before, that's not a small thing; it tells me you've been carrying this in rooms where people were too uncomfortable with pain to simply be present in it with you. You don't have to make yourself smaller here.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't really know what to do with that, honestly. Like, part of me wants to just brush it off and say "it's fine, I'm fine," because that's what I always do. But something about you saying that I don't have to make myself smaller... it's hitting somewhere I wasn't expecting.
therapist: That impulse to say "I'm fine" is so practiced it probably comes before you even decide to say it — but notice that you didn't this time, and that matters. Something in you is choosing to stay with this instead of brushing past it, and that's not nothing; that's actually quite brave. I'm wondering what it feels like in your body right now, in this moment where you're not making yourself smaller.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
